review-20.title: Open mic #20 set notes: LeSlam Comedy, Munich
review-20.summary: Four shows in a row on the same script, listening line by line for where to pause and where to swap a punchline.
body: For my last four open mics I’ve worked from a single script, polishing it and adding to it instead of writing brand-new material. It works well: whatever falls flat one night gets rewritten and tried again the next. Some spots can be fixed. Others never come right however I rework them, and those can probably go.

This time audience members beat me to the punchline several times, and I handled the chatter badly. At one point I paused for the laugh, nothing came, and my mind went blank for two seconds. The first few minutes were fine, then the set sagged in the middle, but luckily the new material near the end went over all right and I clawed my way back. That has never happened to me before. Usually, once a set goes down, it stays down. Strange.

Never put callbacks right next to each other: the audience will see them coming. Don’t treat the audience like idiots.
Reshuffling old bits opens up holes in the logic.
The last word or two of my sentences trail off and are hard to hear.
My mumbling has improved a little.
My pacing is better, and the gaps between sentences seem about right for now, but they still don’t feel natural.
Next week I’m doing a showcase in Hamburg, only my second ever. Out of Munich and heading north!

review-19.title: Open mic #19 set notes: LeSlam Comedy, Munich
review-19.summary: In a bookstore with twenty people in the audience, I could see every face.
body: A lovely open mic. I felt connected to the audience the whole way through, something I hadn’t felt in a long time.

It was actually my second time at the Rhine Bookstore; the first had been more of a soft launch. The space is tiny, just 20 people in the audience, compared with the 40-plus we always had at EineWeltHaus, so you’re right up close and can see every face. The first time I played the bookstore, the room was cold and I felt everyone was scrutinizing me. It was terrifying. This time it went well and I loved it. I still can’t tell whether small rooms or big ones are better. Stand-up remains a dark art!

My pacing was uneven. I deliberately slowed down and left room for laughs, but the rhythm still felt off in lots of places. I chatted with the audience too much, and some of that chat had no jokes in it, which broke the flow. I blanked on lines three times. I hadn’t properly relearned my old material, so I stumbled over it and buried several punchlines myself. I didn’t know what to do with my hands: one minute I was fiddling with the mic cable, the next they were in my pockets. And I ended far too many sentences with “ah”, which was painful to listen to.

The bits about the immigration office and about my bad German and English have each been done four or five times now and are fairly reliable. They’re keepers, and I can add more jokes to them later. The kao bei bit (Taiwanese slang for “damn it”, though the characters literally read “near the north”) is wildly inconsistent: sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t. A few spots in the new material got laughs, so those can stay.
Nineteen sets in, I seem to be developing a slightly better sense of what actually counts as a joke. I hope that’s the start of real progress. Keep at it, on to the next one...

review-18.title: Open mic #18 set notes: LeSlam Comedy, Munich
review-18.summary: Writing new material on the flight home, and getting a bit I’d done four times to sprout a new punchline.
body: I opened the show. I got through a script of 2,000-plus Chinese characters in 12 minutes, which is fast. The weaker the audience reaction, the faster I went, and I barely left them any room to laugh.

Overall it went OK, and certainly much better than the last time I opened. This crowd wasn’t big on laughing, but they were listening intently. Two young women in the front row (girls, really) carried the energy of the room and were seriously funny themselves. Someone from my home region told me we were funnier than open mics back in China, which made me happy. And for the first time ever, an audience member asked for a photo with me. Happy again.

The material spanned three generations. Going home to China is an endless source of material, so I wrote some new stuff about bombing at an open mic in Harbin, plus bits comparing Germany with Northeast China. The middle section I’d done once before in Harbin, so this was its second outing. The last part was material I’d done more than four times; I know it well and it takes no brainpower. Even so, I somehow left out a crucial part of my oldest bit. Honestly, I’m impressed with myself.

This was probably the least polished set I’ve ever done. I wrote most of the new material on the flight back and skipped the script-reading session. Writing jokes is a perfect fit for long-haul flights: write them, run them a few times, and hours have passed. A few of the jokes went over reasonably well, so the effort wasn’t wasted.

I’m getting more used to cold rooms. They still affect my pacing, but much less than before. That’s something I picked up from comedians back in Harbin: if the room is cold, it’s cold, and I do my thing. A comedian’s state and rhythm shouldn’t be thrown too much by the room. Deep down I obviously want the room to explode, but what I deliver should be the same regardless.

Another thing I was pleased about: I added a punchline to an old bit I’d done three or four times. Just one line, but it worked far better than I expected. Who knew an old tree could still put out new shoots? That spot had always been so-so. Running the script the day before, I realized the logic didn’t quite hold, so I swapped in a punchline that followed more naturally, and the laugh came. That’s a good approach, and I can use it to rework other old bits.

For the past few months I’ve felt stuck on a plateau. This script taught me two things. One is what I just described. The other sounds too obvious to be worth saying: punchlines have to be crafted more cleverly. Looking back at my earlier scripts, many lines I thought were jokes didn’t get laughs, and on closer inspection they were just amusing turns of phrase, not real jokes. Once an open mic proves something isn’t funny, replace it as soon as possible. Whether I’m able to replace it is another question, but I can’t be precious about it. Starting from those two points, maybe I can break through the plateau, at least a little.
I did both this open mic and the one in Harbin jet-lagged. This time was even more hardcore: I landed one day and was on stage the next evening. I guess I really do love stand-up 😂

review-16.title: Showcase 1 – OpenMic#016: a mixed bag
review-16.summary: My first showcase: a 3,700-character script stretched over 22 minutes and 41 seconds.
body: To keep count of my stage appearances, I’ve still labeled this open mic #16, even though it was showcase #1.
My first showcase, my sixteenth time on stage. I did 22 minutes and 41 seconds from a 3,700-character script, using every stand-up trick I’ve learned so far.

I have nothing but respect for anyone who can do a 60-minute solo show, and anyone who can be relentlessly funny for 60 minutes, I bow down to. These twenty-odd minutes wiped me out; I got home and collapsed. Just running the script four or five times before and after the show left me utterly exhausted. Work was intense that week too: every evening I got home after seven, grabbed something to eat and rewrote the script until midnight. A change in the lineup meant I had to fill more time, so I crammed another 1,500 characters into what had been a 2,200-character script.

The show went so-so. The first few minutes were good, then it slowly sank. By the middle a few people had their heads down, and some were on their phones. Watching the video afterward, I think by the second half both the audience and I were tired. The good news is that for the first time I felt I could breathe on stage. It was subtle and brief, but beautiful: in that moment I was relaxed and genuinely enjoying the stage. Then there were the groaners, like brownies and LeBron James (in Chinese the two names share the sound “bulang”). I knew few people would laugh, but I wanted to do them anyway. Three or five people laughed, and I was perfectly content.

I also noticed that strong material works in any room, while average material is wildly inconsistent. The cake-eating bit I did last December absolutely killed that night; yesterday it did just OK. I forget whose podcast it was, but someone said a truly great bit works in 99% of rooms. I don’t have anything like that yet. Three of my last four shows were fairly cold, and in two of them I did my relatively stronger old material, so clearly I need to keep working on the writing. I feel I’ve hit a plateau and don’t know how to get better. Stand-up is wearing me out, too: the workload is almost a full-time job. Conveniently, I’m going home to China on vacation in September. I’ll take a break and be back at it in October!

review-15.title: LeSlam Comedy Munich open mic #15: set notes
review-15.summary: In the small room at the Rhine Bookstore, trying to work out which bits to rework and which to let go.
body: For the first time, Munich’s Chinese-language open mic wasn’t held at EWH (EineWeltHaus). This was a trial run at the Rhine Bookstore, with about half the usual audience.

The first half was a bit cold. I was on second and already nervous going up. My set was long, 2,200-plus characters, made up of bits I want to do at the showcase, mostly old material. I forgot an entire section again, and there’s one spot I’ve now forgotten at two open mics in a row, which suggests it should be cut. Dementia is a disease, and I need treatment.

The new material got a lukewarm response across the board, so I’ll cut it as needed. My two strongest old bits are basically reliable. This was the first time I really felt what an open mic is for: testing material. If something fails to get laughs several times running, and it isn’t what I really want to say anyway, I should boldly kill it. Anything with a chance of being saved, I keep reworking. I’ll judge from the video.

The new material came in the middle, and that’s where the set fell apart. I didn’t notice when I was writing it, but the video showed the setups and logic really were weak. By that point I was uncomfortable, talking fast and tense. Strangely, the moment I reached the old material I settled down. I was visibly more relaxed on stage, gesturing and starting to wander around. It was interesting not to feel the set getting worse and worse. That’s the advantage of old material: it’s all muscle memory, the lines take up no RAM, so I can pay attention to other things. And happily, I added a few new tags to that last old bit, and they went over well. Rewriting old material is hard. So far it’s all down to inspiration; I can’t do it at all with the comedy formulas from the books or any other technique.
Thanks to the Rhine Bookstore for hosting us! And I’m looking forward to the showcase next weekend.

review-15-rehearsal.title: OpenMic#015: showcase rehearsal
review-15-rehearsal.summary: A rehearsal checklist, noting item by item which lines landed and which setups were still unclear.
body:
Landed:
- Kao bei
- Primary to middle school, associate degree to bachelor’s
- Always picking the fields that don’t pay
- The boss
	- “Bichi” (bitch)
	- “The urge is back”
	- Business trip to Paris (didn’t really work)
- 240 decibels
- My uncle calls me “big bro”
- West Germany, the Soviet Union
	- Didn’t land: in Germany, we call the Germans “foreigners”; no sense of boundaries
- Errenzhuan (Northeastern folk duet theater)
- East and West Germany merging

Didn’t land:
- Tieling
- Studying for a master’s
- Not replying to comments on my WeChat account, because I don’t know the answers either
- The stand-up disconnect: English plus stand-up jargon
	- Visibility: stand-up TV shows
		- Change it to “Am I a ghost?”
	- Value: stand-up doesn’t preach
	- Got a reaction:
		- Preening and smirking
		- The run of parallel lines about open mics
		- Take offline: stand-up goes live
		- Fired: “I can be on fire”
- Scumbag, piece of scum: setup unclear
- The kneeling German
	- Setup unclear
	- Got a reaction:
		- “Weren’t you hot stuff before?”
		- “Finally standing tall in front of the foreigners”
		- “My Young Pioneer red scarf glowed even redder”
- Making noises with my mouth:
	- Got a reaction: can’t get it into gear
	- No reaction: DJ scratching, beatboxing
- “This is Germany, it has to be in German”: the turn at the end didn’t land
- “So what if I talk about that stuff?”
- “What are you showing off for abroad? Hearing it just eats you up inside”
	- But the later line, “What the hell does being 180 cm tall have to do with you?”, worked OK

review-14.title: LeSlam Comedy Munich open mic #14: set notes
review-14.summary: After forgetting an entire section, looking back at my pace, my pauses and the punchlines drowned in filler.
body: This one went OK.

Bombing at the last open mic had left its mark. Before going on, I was afraid of falling back into that spiral: the colder the room, the more I rush; the more I rush, the colder the room. As a result I talked a bit fast and slipped back into my habits from when I started doing open mics last year: no pauses, plowing on before the laugh had even died down.
And this was the first time I skipped an entire section… I’ve forgotten lines plenty of times, but jumping a whole chunk was a first! No wonder the time seemed to fly by when I came off stage.

This show saw the return of Mantou, the final boss. His setups and punchlines are incredibly clear. By the time a punchline is coming, the audience is already rubbing their hands, ready for it, and the moment it lands, the room goes off. It’s like stage diving at a concert: he walks to the edge, strikes a pose, jumps, and the crowd catches him safely. Of course, the jokes themselves are cleverly written too; otherwise he’d jump and everyone would step aside.

As for me, my setups are often off, or the punchlines aren’t strong enough, so they slip past without the audience noticing. I have to say it again about Munich audiences: at more than 90% of shows they’re incredibly supportive, practically starving for it, just waiting for your punchline. If the joke is funny, they will react. We’re lucky to have audiences like that.

Also, a lot of people didn’t know “Arbeit macht frei” or Dachau, so the reaction there was lukewarm. A few spots were inside jokes, stuff about comedians doing solo specials online versus live, which left people who don’t watch much stand-up completely lost.

I keep wanting to throw in an extra line or phrase on the spot, with mixed results. There’s far too much filler, which comes straight from not knowing my lines well enough. Too much filler makes the punchlines less crisp and the meaning murky, and the laughs get buried under a pile of useless words.
On to the next one

review-14-notes.title: OpenMic#014: how stand-up has changed me
review-14-notes.summary: Reviewing set 14 line by line, noting which setups need filling in and where to leave space.
body: OpenMic#014: how stand-up has changed me

- American valley girl, vocal fry, uptalk: what’s so cool about that? Speak Chinese in that tone and it’s just a Liaoning accent (a Northeastern accent). That’s exactly how my uncle talks. Act-out: English industry jargon matched with Northeastern slang

- Go easy on slip-of-the-tongue jokes: “copying bits”, not “learning bits”
- Acronyms: play up how painful it is not to understand them, so the payoff is funnier; act out a speaker firing off these acronyms, make it grating to listen to
- Make the hosting part even more awkward
- Mention that the roundtable has lots of older people; with that setup in place, what follows flows better
- Too much filler:
	- Learn the script properly;
	- Improvise less
	- No final draft; lots of lines weren’t settled
- Too fast: “hobbies: stripping”, same as “balance”: leave a gap, and there can be two laughs
- Go easy on the dark humor: Arbeit macht frei
	- Add a hint
	- People didn’t dare laugh, or didn’t get it
	- I came across as coy
- Indian accent: hold the second line a beat? Or drop it
- Forgot an entire section
- Change to “I’m an audio engineer, and I’m also a stand-up comedian. Before I’d even finished, the crowd went wild with applause. Killing on the second line, that might be the funniest I’ve ever been”
	- Too much filler in the middle; the punchline wasn’t crisp, and the laugh got washed out
- Change to “That was the year Jay Chou debuted”, because saying it came from that year’s hottest newcomer could mean I sang it yesterday, not necessarily more than twenty years ago
- MD and PM need explaining
- “Have you all watched the stand-up shows online? Those of us who do live comedy, xxx.” Explain the difference between online and live to the audience, xxx
- Big laughs:
	- Wu Jing impression, Indian accent
	- MNHLKXJ: the pinyin initials of Munich LeSlam Comedy
	- Thomas flair: an audience member said “do one”, crowd work, but actually a prepared joke
	- “Widowed / you look like an animal”: acted out well
-

review-nonhero.title: The non-hero: playing low status
review-nonhero.summary: Going through the bits that got laughs, and thinking about how the me on stage relates to the audience.
body: Something I’ve realized recently about my material: I don’t lower myself enough. I don’t give the audience a sense of superiority; I don’t present myself as a non-hero.

I’m always ranting about and attacking some group of people, and if that isn’t handled well, it comes across as showing off: look how great I am, I’ve exposed some social reality, I alone am awake while the world sleeps.

My bits that work:
- Bombing in Frankfurt
- Being fed cake by Tuco
- My bad English
- Watching porn as a kid
- German city hall
- My asshole relatives
Apart from the bad English and the porn, these are all really about me being “unlucky”: I ran into idiots.

A while ago I saw someone analyzing the comedian Han Gao. His technique is trying to look cool and failing. My Frankfurt bombing bit is exactly that, and it gives the audience a lovely sense of superiority: wow, I’d never do something that dumb, I’m better than him.

German city hall and my asshole relatives are both revenge stories. First I get screwed, I’m the non-hero; then I get my revenge and become the hero. I’m not sure ending up as the hero is a good thing, but audiences go for it, maybe because it’s so relatable. Everyone hates German bureaucrats and obnoxious relatives, so watching me win gives them the rush of a revenge fantasy.
Actually, the bad English is a non-hero bit too, because my bad English made me do lots of stupid things. The porn bit may work simply because the topic is racy and I tell the story vividly.

Besides Han Gao, I just listened to Han Dagou interviewing the comedian Zihan Wang. She said her first solo show was about how weird other people are, and her second was about how weird she is. That’s also a move toward lowering yourself, and audiences naturally warm to it more.

review-13.title: LeSlam Comedy Munich open mic #13: what am I even doing this for?
review-13.summary: The minutes after I opened the show, as the room slowly went cold, and the question I asked myself afterward.
body: Set done, and once again it’s time to ask myself: what am I even doing this for?

I opened this time. When I started doing stand-up I always asked to go first. The logic: the sooner you die, the sooner you’re reborn. Waiting is torture, and once you’re done you can sit back and enjoy everyone else.

I started the way I always do, with random stuff: chatting about the World Cup, about open mics and comedians, plus whatever else popped into my head, none of it funny. I can’t even remember what I said. The response was lukewarm. On a whim I threw in an old bit to get the audience warmed up faster. But I didn’t remember parts of it well, and I stumbled my way into my prepared material. By then I was getting flustered. A couple of bits later, people started trickling into the front row. Not that they wanted the front row; it was the only row with free seats. The room got a bit distracted, and on a whim again, I went into crowd work. Awkward. Extremely awkward. When I’m nervous and frazzled I get very aggressive, and the guy in the front row was so startled he started stammering. Sorry, man!
A friendly reminder: please arrive on time, or a certain male LeSlam comedian will pick on you relentlessly 🤪

Back to the material. The room went completely silent, from lukewarm to cold, in sympathy with the air conditioning. As English-speaking comics say, I lost the room. My pacing and pauses fell apart, and I got through the rest on muscle memory alone.

Afterward I was actually fine; it was just those few minutes on stage that were hard to bear. Once this script was written, I don’t think I especially liked it. Maybe the subject was too stale, and since I was opening, I’d mentally prepared for a cold room. I just didn’t expect it to be that cold. Huge thanks to the comedians who came after me and killed. You got that room seriously hot!

Lots of mistakes here I can avoid next time: don’t ramble about random stuff, and don’t do crowd work for the hell of it. And when the audience doesn’t react, keep your cool: the more panicked you feel, the more your pacing falls apart.
Special thanks to Xiaozhi, whose hosting was electric and whose riffing was brilliant. And thanks to our veteran Ziheng for coming all that way. Come to Munich more often!
On to the next one…

review-12.title: Open mic #12: set notes
review-12.summary: When the room is hot, how do you treat the audience as friends and still leave enough room for the laughs?
body: Of all the Chinese-language open mics I’ve done in Munich, this one had the best vibe ever, in the audience and among the comedians alike. The room was as hot as last December’s show, and the comedians were all on form. Everyone seemed comfortable up there, and you could see they were enjoying the stage. Several of them have found their stage persona and a way of talking that feels natural to them. You guys are amazing!

Right from the start you could tell the room was hot. The audience kept reacting, and watching from the side I relaxed a little. My set went pretty well. There were a few places where I’d planned crowd work; when writing, I’d decided to see how the room felt before committing. The room was hot and some audience members were chiming in on their own, so I did a bit of crowd work, and the riffing went fairly well. One lesson from this riffing: when you feel you can’t keep it going, get out fast! Either move on to the next person or go back to your material. Grinding away only gets more and more awkward. Don’t ask me how I know.

I talked a bit fast this time and didn’t leave room for laughs in a few places. I need to watch that and stop rushing to blurt everything out. But I don’t really know how to get it right: in the past I’ve left lots of space, the pace dropped and the room went cold. A dark art!

This was probably the fastest I’ve ever written a first draft. I mentioned the idea while chatting with friends and immediately wanted to write it. I posted the rough premise in the comedians’ group chat, everyone thought it was fun, and I finished the first draft that same night. But revising it was unusually hard. Nothing I changed felt right, and it was really frustrating. Only a week before the open mic did I finally sort out the logic and add several more punchlines. Along the way my friends gave me two great ideas, one structural from LadyWendy and one big punchline from forever. I used both and they worked really well. And thanks to Jianzhu Jianbing Xuezhang for guidance on content vetting. Much respect 👊

The line that has stuck with me most recently: connect with the audience; treat them as friends. It sounds like a platitude. I’ve turned it into two practical steps. First, mindset: don’t go up chasing a kill; I’m just testing material, so lower my expectations. Second, know the script cold. Taking the second one first: the brain only has so much capacity. On stage you’re extremely nervous, and there’s so much to process: the lights, the audience, the venue, noise from outside. If you don’t know your script, you spend most of your time up there trying to remember lines, and beforehand you keep worrying about forgetting them, which makes you even more nervous. Knowing the script is the precondition.

Back to the first step. Trust that repeated reminders and pep talks to yourself can work. This set had parts that went well, parts that were flat, and punchlines I’d designed that got nothing, but none of it rattled me much, because I was mentally prepared. At the script-reading session, people had already pointed out that some parts might not be funny or appropriate (like the gay bit), but I wanted to stick with them and try them out, just to see whether they’d work. When you’re steady, at the very least your connection with the audience won’t snap straight away. Then again, all of this held up because the room was hot and our host, German Crossover Roundtable, was great. I think both points hold in a cold room too; it’s just harder to see the results.
On to the next one!

review-9-11.title: Open mics #9–11: set notes
review-9-11.summary: My first time hosting and my first bit about age anxiety: looking back at three very different nights on stage.
body: Number nine was my first time hosting, number ten was about age anxiety, and No. 11 was about my bad foreign languages. No. 12 is coming up this week, with more dirty jokes.

Hosting for the first time made me even more nervous than my first time doing a set. I prepared a lot, watched lots of videos and read up, and even wrote special material for the links between acts. It’s different from doing your own set, where good or bad, it’s your own business. As host you’re responsible for the whole show and mustn’t wreck the other comedians’ sets. I felt completely unsure of myself. I knew that stage fairly well, but I had no idea what hosting on it would be like. The crowd work was a disaster: I managed to chill the whole room. Luckily the comedians that night were great and warmed it back up, act by act. In the second half I was much more relaxed. I could riff a bit on the comedians’ material and slot in the bits I’d prepared. The other reason is that I stopped doing crowd work in the second half… I was a bit scared.

Another thing about hosting: how are the comedians done so quickly? Stay up there a bit longer, I haven’t caught my breath! Even offstage your brain has to keep working, scanning the comedians’ material for anything you can riff on. Crowd work has its techniques, too, and it takes experience. I recently came across some tips I found helpful: ask yes-or-no questions rather than open ones (otherwise you may not be able to run with the answer, unless you’re a crowd-work god), and for jobs or relationships you can sort the answers into a few broad types and have something ready for each, etc.

It took me a whole day to work up the nerve to watch the video of my hosting. At the start I relentlessly picked on a couple who came in late and sat in the front row. I was like a madman. If I’d been in the audience, I’d have wanted to go up and smack me myself. I was being such a pest. My apologies to you both!

In March I talked about age anxiety. I was really happy to be able to talk about it at all. I’ve had age anxiety for a few years; for a while I wouldn’t even tell people my real age when socializing. Since I started talking about it, it has got much better. Stand-up really does have healing powers. This set went so-so, and I felt bad afterward. Doing it felt like punching cotton: all that effort and nothing to push against. I’m deeply narcissistic and usually rewatch my sets over and over, but this video is probably my second-least-watched, after the Frankfurt one. I wasn’t in the right state before I went on, either. Maybe I was tired from too much socializing that weekend, and I was on last, so by the time I got up there I felt drained. I recently went over the video and the script again, and I think the problem was that I wanted to say too much, the emotion wasn’t clear, and I kept circling a small point that wasn’t very relatable and had no jokes in it, so naturally I lost my connection with the audience. Speaking of connection, a riff at the very start didn’t land and I went straight into my material, so the audience never really got into it from the beginning. Build a connection, build a connection! I’ve heard it over and over lately. Once the audience accepts you as a person, the rest is easy; without that connection, even tearing a washbasin in half with your bare hands won’t be enough.

Then there was the last one, number eleven, in April. I was in great form, on a par with last December. Looking back at both, the key was that I fully connected with the audience. Both times I started with small throwaway jokes, riffing, and calling out the comedians and the host before getting into my material. The audience relaxed, I relaxed, and everything after that could make sense. I forgot lines like crazy, but I hadn’t realized that forgetting a line can also be a way to get a laugh. In the middle I tried crowd work again, and again it was incredibly awkward. Luckily, before I passed out, I said: “You can all see this crowd work is going terribly.” That reconnected me with the audience. Everyone laughed, I got a buzz, and I was much more relaxed after that. I’m still struck by how a live stand-up show is pieced together from countless random events. If I hadn’t named the elephant in the room right then, things might have got heavier and heavier, and it all came down to a split second. That’s the magic of live performance, not just in stand-up but in music too.

This was my first time doing dirty jokes. It didn’t go too badly, but compared with my earlier material it was clearly weaker. When we talked it over afterward, we agreed that dirty jokes are risky, like being the dealer in mahjong: you win double or lose double. Being dirty for the sake of it is just vulgar; being dirty to get a laugh, or to make a point or convey a feeling, is fine, I think. We can talk about food, clothes, housing and getting around, eating, drinking and bodily functions, work and life, joys and worries, so why not sex and things related to it? Those topics can’t be aired online in China, but plenty of people do them in live shows, not to mention English-language stand-up. When a dirty joke offends people, the original sin is that it isn’t funny (to quote Yanyan Lin).

Lately nearly all my free time has gone to stand-up: watching all kinds of videos, listening to all kinds of podcasts, writing all kinds of jokes. I’ve dropped AI, stopped playing guitar, stopped exercising. Am I trying to go pro or what? I’ve also noticed that the more jokes I write, the more each one feels like a jigsaw piece, and what they add up to is me. Besides digging things out of my memory, writing makes me step back and observe my own opinions and emotions, and it seems to help me understand myself better. I learned this from Zilong, of the Zilong Comedy Workshop, when he gave us a training session a while ago: keep asking yourself why you think the way you do. Bo Yu said something similar. When he was writing his solo show, he kept asking himself: What makes you so special? Everyone has been through this, so why should you be the one to write about it? What makes you so special?

A sudden thought: I want to write a book… no, wait, I mean I want to do a solo show. That’s a huge challenge, because after ten open mics, all my funny material put together probably doesn’t add up to five minutes. But you need something to work toward. In 2026, I’ll keep performing and keep digging.

review-7-8.title: Open mics #7–8: my 2025 in review
review-7-8.summary: From Munich to Frankfurt: looking back on a year of eight sets.
body: I did stand-up eight times this year: seven open mics in Munich and one in Frankfurt. Almost every set was new material; my urge to write was off the charts. I went from fumbling about clueless at the first one to eventually closing the show, and at the last one I killed (or so I felt). That dopamine rush is unbeatable. For a moment I felt possessed by the comedian Kamu. It was a stark contrast to bombing in Frankfurt, and that’s the magic of stand-up. At the end, Jiaotang even gave me an award for “male comedian with the best attendance”. Accepting it, I said stand-up is an escape hatch from my life. Then I explained that my life isn’t actually that miserable, it’s fine, really, though the more I explained, the less anyone believed me. Every Sunday evening, when the thought of work on Monday brings on that Sunday blue feeling, I write jokes, and the Sunday blue becomes the Sunday blues.

The agony of being stuck while writing; the “I’m a genius” feeling after coming up with a (self-proclaimed) brilliant punchline; the nerves before going on; the release of pressure coming off; and, during those five minutes on stage when I’m fully engaged, slipping out of the real world through an emergency exit: all of these are wonderful and rare experiences. Five minutes on stage is a luxury. With one microphone and one mouth, you get fifty strangers to listen intently as you sketch out a world, and if it works, they laugh and applaud. Maybe only sex gives faster positive feedback (or slower).

Stand-up has also made me more real: facing painful past experiences head on, like the teacher who beat students, the sharp-tongued relatives and the idiot colleagues, turning them into bits and leaving those memories on stage; facing my age anxiety more calmly; being more honest about my own feelings and thoughts. I still can’t show my truest self on stage. I don’t have that much courage yet, and my technique isn’t there yet either. In 2026 we’ll take it slowly. After all, unlike Chinese workplaces, stand-up has no “you’re out at 35” rule. You can keep doing it until you die.

On the technical side there’s still a lot to improve: how to talk comfortably, how and where to leave pauses, how to make punchlines crisper. I tried act-outs and they felt good, but I need to let go more. In the new year I plan to try English open mics. Munich probably has more English open mics than any other city in Germany (not sure about Berlin), with shows almost every day. Besides getting more stage time, I’m quietly hoping to improve my English, and my confidence speaking it. I’ve written some material and found I have no idea where the laughs are in English. I’ll need to bomb a few times to really find out.

Thanks to Jiaotang’s three bosses, Nazhua, Shaodong and Lin, for building a stage for us amateurs. It may look like a hobby, but a lot of thought and effort goes on behind the scenes. They’ve created a safe, comfortable and, above all, professional environment for the comedians on stage and the audience below, so the comedians can be as funny as they like and the audience can just enjoy themselves.
Whenever life isn’t going your way, think of stand-up!

review-6.title: Open mic #6: set notes
review-6.summary: Trying out analogies at a themed open mic, and trying to get my rhythm back after the audience talked back.
body: Before going on, I watched a live set by the comedian Xinzai about forgetting his lines at a corporate gig. I thought, I’d better not forget mine. And I didn’t, exactly: I mixed them up. Last open mic I also had a slip of the tongue; this time there was one fewer. The setup was hard to deliver to begin with, and once I got it wrong the audience was totally lost.

This was a stand-up show co-hosted with a dating event, so we had to stick to a theme. I talked about how work is like dating, then ranted about work. It was the first time I wrote material starting from an opinion and an emotion instead of a story. Very interesting, and not easy to write. I compared work and dating, then put workplace things into dating scenarios. I think that technique is called a mix, or is it fish out of water? Either way, I can keep writing like this.
This time I did more crowd work and more callbacks to other comedians, and it went well. To the guy Maidi picked on: sorry for saying you were old, the script made me do it 😂

The price of crowd work is that the rhythm gets messy: afterward you need time to remember your lines. I didn’t even notice I’d said something wrong. The audience was trying to guess what I was getting at, and I was trying to guess why they weren’t laughing. From that point the energy started to sag. I got nervous and the filler increased. In several places I also left too much room for the audience to react, which threw off the rhythm too.

Also, things that seem funny on paper may only be funny as writing; spoken aloud, they fall a bit short. I like parallel structures, maybe a lingering after-effect of the argumentative essays and lyrical prose I wrote for the gaokao, China’s university entrance exam. Having tried them up to now, I’m giving them up. A bit needs an overall framework, but these small rhetorical structures don’t seem to do anything in stand-up; at least in my experience they have no effect.

Next time, if I can’t write a new script, I’d like to string together the bits that have worked before. If remembering the lines doesn’t take up too much brainpower, I can add some crowd work. If I write new material, I’ll try to narrow the scope and keep hitting one topic with jokes, expressing one emotion. Too many topics and scenes, jumping back and forth, and the audience gets distracted and can’t get into it. If I can’t pull that off, never mind: I’ll keep what tested reasonably well and dig deeper.

I have to say, vibe is a mysterious thing. Every live show is made up of countless random events: the audience’s mood, the comedians’ mood, the length of the show, the running order, one line said wrong, one look that hits just right, the temperature and ventilation in the room, how loud the sound system is… and there I go again with the parallel structures. The day before yesterday I went to see a band, and one of the members said that in ten years AI might replace humans at writing music, but it can’t replace live music, can’t replace the temporary community we form by getting together. Stand-up is the same. You never know what’s going to happen before you go on, and whether a joke lands is more like a random event. It’s a thrill, and it’s one of the reasons the stand-up stage is so addictive. The most important reason, though, is the sense of achievement you get from making other people laugh.
Also, where’s the amazing Kaka? Munich stand-up needs you!

review-5.title: Open mic #5: set notes
review-5.summary: Back on stage after three months, I found that the toilet in the audience’s heads wasn’t the one I was describing.
body: Back on stage after three months. Even though it was my fifth time, I was super nervous beforehand. Afterward came a huge release. Honestly, I quite like that feeling. Maybe I’m a masochist.

Overall it went reasonably well. A few lines I thought were jokes didn’t get a response. Going over it with friends afterward, I realized some of them weren’t relatable enough. For example, I complained that the English abbreviation “repo” is weird, and people thought, what’s wrong with that, we all say it. I also hadn’t laid out my premise clearly, so people didn’t know what I was ranting about and were just confused. Worst of all, I made two slips of the tongue in that one spot: instead of saying the abbreviation drops a third of the word, I said it keeps a third, and instead of “the audience writes repo” I said “the comedians”. If I can’t even say it right, how is the audience supposed to laugh?

Slips of the tongue are fine; practice will fix them. But the premise is crucial. The audience needs to know clearly what you’re talking about and what you’re trying to say; only then can they let their guard down and follow your emotion. The logic has to hold up too, or people will be baffled. I have to say, laying out a premise clearly in as few words as possible is incredibly hard.

Then there’s the smart flushing toilet. I was ranting about the kind that only flushes, but my friend thought I meant the kind that washes and dries you. With that misunderstanding, nothing I said afterward made sense. That’s another case of an unclear premise.

Another thing: if what you’re saying isn’t your real emotion, holes appear easily. What I actually wanted to rant about was people demanding special treatment, but that wasn’t easy to say on stage, so I switched to a different angle and watered down my real feeling. And then I had to change the setup. When neither the premise nor the emotion is real, the logic tends to break down, and the audience feels you don’t know what you’re talking about. Keep it real!
Also, don’t do too many puns and wordplay. Unless they’re really cleverly constructed, use a couple at the start to warm up the room and leave it at that.

Today I met an audience member who has seen all of our open mics and even knew my opening line. I was a little moved. When I called you out in a riff, I didn’t expect to get applause, my one and only round of applause (blushes). So you have to keep coming, Kaka!

review-1-4.title: My first four open mics: a recap
review-1-4.summary: From my first open mic in February to my fourth: counting the laughs I expected and the ones I didn’t.
body: Since my first open mic back in February, I’ve done four in total. It has been an amazing experience, and I felt I should write a short recap.

My love of stand-up goes back to 2016, when I started watching Tonight 80’s Talk Show. The “80s” in the name, meaning China’s post-’80s generation, is interesting: back then it stood for a rebellious generation, and years later that generation has turned into the aunties and uncles of Xiaohongshu. At the time I didn’t find the show all that funny, but it introduced me to stand-up comedy as a genre. After that I started watching English-language stand-up: Fluffy, Russell Peters, Ali Wong, Jimmy, and later the Chinese shows Roast! and Rock & Roast.

At first I didn’t mean to get up and do it myself; I just wanted to be close to it. In 2022 I went to a stand-up meetup in Munich and met Nazhua, who kept urging me to get on stage. Only this January, when I’d written a script, did I finally decide to do it. Once I got up there, I discovered you shouldn’t touch this stuff: one hit and you’re hooked. Now I can relate to a certain first-generation king of Chinese stand-up.

I was extremely nervous before my first time, because I had no idea what it would feel like up there. Maybe inspired by Doudou Hu, I asked to go first. The logic: the sooner you die, the sooner you’re reborn. It went smoothly, I was fairly relaxed, and there was even a bit of interaction with the audience. How to put it? Everything was fine, except there weren’t really any laughs. Honestly, my goal the first time was not to forget my lines and just get through it. I love stand-up so much that getting on stage once fulfilled a long-held wish. And the moment I came off, I wanted to do it again.

The first time I talked about teachers hitting students when I was a kid; the second, the bizarre relatives at banquet tables back home; the third, a bit more of the old relatives material plus running my WeChat Official Account; the fourth, a rant about German bureaucrats. There were bits I thought were super clever that went down cold, and spots I didn’t think were jokes where the audience laughed.
